items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I got Jimmy Cobb on drums who was seventy nine, and I was eighty two. And that was the band I had.

ctx.x: You know, being a musician yourself sometimes screws you up because I'm used to calling six guys, going to a gig, and playing a two hour concert without a rehearsal. Rehearsing is something that I don't know much about. As long as I'm calling the tunes, I hire musicians that know the tunes I know. If I'm working for them, then I gotta know what tunes they are gonna play so I can refresh myself, you know. I don't play that often. So I listen to Muddy Waters play the blues and I know Dizzy Gillespie can play the…

two was Anat,; Howard was forty nine, Randy Brecker came to play the gig; he was sixty four. I got Jimmy Cobb on drums who was seventy nine, and I was eighty two. And that was the band I had. And we had like a ten minute rehearsal, played for a week, two shows a night, and had the ball of our lives. We're all friends and we swung the whole week. Esperanza said, "Let's get that band together again." So that sometimes screws me up as a producer when I ask musicians to do it. Bobby Hackett used to be my man in jam…
Wow. These jam sessions, particularly at the end, I guess is usually when they happen … are there artists that just don't like to do that?

items.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: because you hit with George Wein

ctx.x: Ashley. Wrote the book on the thing. So I – he had lived around there a little while. He was down there doing his thing in the festival. So he had me and Larry Willis on this little talk show right there in the yard. I remember. It was pretty nice. People accepted it. The band sounded good every night. It was great.

That same weekend you hit with George – you were hitting with George – you were really there the whole weekend, because you hit with George Wein. I think Esperanza [Spaulding] was in the band. How do you feel about that, this new generation of players like Esperanza?

I think the talent – all through this music, there’s going to be people that come up and come to the top, because the people love this music. It’s going to always be jazz music. It’s al[ways] going to be. I don’t know how popular it might ever be. It might be like it has always been, up and down, but it’s always going to be here. For me, I can’t see it getting any better than through my life, being all the people that I had an opportunity to see, like Louis Armstrong, to know him and see him play and just be…
